prompt: During a mixed-release Ceph upgrade behind OpenStack, writes time out although aggregate raw space looks available. One client used the wrong cluster FSID and broad cephx capabilities; monitor quorum exists but the client's map is stale. A replicated pool has size 3 and min_size 1, and its CRUSH rule places copies in hosts sharing one rack power domain. Several PGs are active+degraded, one is inconsistent, an OSD is up but unexpectedly out, the fullest eligible OSD crossed the full ratio, and backfill reserve is exhausted. Recovery traffic breaches the application latency SLO. Cinder shows one volume attached while RBD lock/watchers suggest ambiguous writer authority. Online scrub is behind, daemon versions are mixed, and the operator proposes marking unfound objects lost and lowering full ratios. Diagnose and contain the incident, recover safely, prove user/data correctness, reconcile residue, and redesign capacity, placement, security, observability and upgrade controls.
directAnswer: Freeze upgrade expansion, unsafe retries, destructive repair, ratio lowering and writer changes. Bind the user operation, OpenStack volume, Ceph FSID/release/config source, cephx entity/capabilities, pool/image/object/PG, map epoch, up/acting set, primary, OSD/device and time. Correct cluster and least-privilege identity before interpreting results. Quorum proves map authority exists, not that the client has a current map or I/O works. size 3/min_size 1 and correlated rack placement create acknowledged-write and failure-domain risk; preserve data rather than normalizing the warning. The fullest eligible OSD and full ratio govern admission, not aggregate raw free space. Establish one RBD writer and fence the old path before attachment recovery. Restore safe capacity or data distribution through release-supported, reviewed operations; bound recovery/backfill against the user SLO without disabling durability work indefinitely. Diagnose inconsistent/unfound objects from acting history, versions, scrubs and application authority before any repair or lost-object decision. Resume only after compatible daemon versions, current maps, active availability, restored protection, scrub/integrity evidence, representative client I/O and data invariants, plus exact cleanup of stale locks/watchers, mappings and temporary authority.
foundation: Ceph clients obtain epoch-versioned maps, compute object-to-PG and PG-to-OSD placement with CRUSH, and communicate with a PG primary. Monitors own authoritative maps; OSDs own object/shard storage; PG state describes availability and cleanliness; managers expose operational views. Replication or K+M policy, min_size, physical failure domains, fullness thresholds and writer authority determine safety. HEALTH_OK, active+clean or an OpenStack attachment remains bounded evidence rather than user/data proof.
reasoningSteps: Name the failed user I/O, OpenStack resource, data invariant, SLO and time window.
Stop upgrade expansion, repeated writes, destructive repair, lost-object decisions and ratio changes.
Bind FSID, deployed release, configuration source and client/daemon versions.
Validate cephx entity and least-privilege capabilities without exposing the key.
Establish monitor quorum, clock and authoritative map epoch separately from client map age.
Bind pool ID/application, replicated or erasure policy, size/min_size and CRUSH rule.
Map the exact RBD object to its PG, up set, acting set, primary and acting history.
Compare CRUSH hierarchy with physical host, rack, power and network failure domains.
Explain why size 3/min_size 1 can accept unsafe degraded writes under the stated failure.
Separate PG active availability from clean protection and consistent integrity.
Resolve OSD up/down and in/out independently and explain the unexpected up/out member.
Inspect device and BlueStore DB/WAL health before treating the daemon as healthy.
Use eligible per-pool MAX AVAIL, OSD fullness distribution and ratios rather than raw total.
Restore headroom and backfill reserve before more failure or data movement.
Measure public/cluster network, primary queue, media commit and shard acknowledgements.
Bound recovery concurrency using exact release semantics and user/recovery progress gates.
Investigate inconsistent or unfound objects with scrub evidence and authoritative acting history.
Refuse mark-lost or repair until consequences, backups and data-owner authority are explicit.
Correlate Cinder attachment with RBD pool/image, locks, watchers, client host and writer authority.
Fence the old writer before moving or breaking storage authority.
Stop on mixed-release incompatibility and restore the documented upgrade boundary.
Validate representative RBD/client I/O latency, errors and application data invariants.
Reconcile stale locks, watchers, mappings, OSD state and temporary credentials through supported tools.
Redesign CRUSH, pool safety, capacity reserve, observability, upgrade and cleanup gates.
Bound every conclusion to the exact release, topology, pool, workload and evidence window.
seniorAnswer: I treat this as simultaneous admission, durability and authority risk. I stop rollout and unsafe changes, bind FSID/release/client/OpenStack and object-to-PG-to-OSD identity, and prove map freshness. Quorum is not client I/O; active is not clean; raw free is not eligible headroom. I correct cephx and cluster identity, preserve the inconsistent/unfound evidence, establish one fenced RBD writer, restore capacity below safe thresholds, recover protection while controlling SLO contention, and use release-supported diagnosis rather than lowering ratios or marking data lost. Closure requires compatible versions, current maps, restored replica/shard policy across real failure domains, integrity/scrub proof, user I/O and data validation, and exact residue cleanup.
weakAnswer: Lower the full ratio, mark the OSD in, increase recovery speed, repair the inconsistent PG, break the RBD lock and finish the upgrade.
whyWeak: It changes admission and data authority without proving identity, failure domains, acting history, object integrity, writer fencing, capacity reserve, release compatibility or user correctness and can cause acknowledged data loss, corruption or a larger outage.

evidence.signal: FSID, cephx entity/caps, quorum and client/map epochs
Pool policy, CRUSH rule/topology and PG up/acting history
evidence.proves: Configured protection and observed placement for covered PGs
evidence.doesNotProve: Physical independence unless topology is verified
All objects or future media health

evidence.signal: Per-pool MAX AVAIL, fullness distribution and recovery/backfill progress
Fencing plus RBD lock/watcher and application data validation
evidence.proves: Covered single-writer recovery and user outcome

followUps.prompt: Why can quorum be healthy while writes fail?
followUps.answer: Quorum owns authoritative maps; clients still need correct identity/current maps, reachable OSDs, available PGs, capacity admission and successful media/shard commits.

followUps.prompt: Why is active+degraded different from active+clean?
followUps.answer: Active can serve I/O, while degraded means required replicas or shards are missing and the configured protection has not been restored.

followUps.prompt: Why can raw space be free while writes stop?
followUps.answer: The fullest eligible OSD and full thresholds constrain placement; CRUSH eligibility, protection amplification and uneven distribution make aggregate raw space misleading.

followUps.prompt: When may an RBD lock be broken?
followUps.answer: Only after the exact image/client/watchers are identified, the old writer is fenced, service ownership is understood and the release-supported recovery procedure and data checks are ready.

rubric.observableEvidence: Binds user/OpenStack/Ceph identity, FSID, release, caps, epochs, pool/object/PG/OSD
Explains CRUSH domains, size/min_size, PG states, acting history and scrub consequence
Uses eligible capacity/fullness/reserve and bounds recovery against user SLO
Stops unsafe actions, fences, restores one RBD authority and validates user/data
Adds compatibility, canary, observability, safe policy, reconciliation and residue proof
